claim: The activity of the lower-limb muscles accounts for most of the metabolic energy cost needed to walk or run.
source: the activity of the lower-limb muscles accounts for most of the metabolic energy cost needed to walk or run (Kram and Taylor, 1990; Kram, 2000; Dickinson et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kram and Taylor, 1990; Kram, 2000; Dickinson et al., 2000

claim: Running is characterized by a spring-like interaction of the body with the ground.
source: Running is characterized by a spring-like interaction of the body with the ground, indicating a significant conversion of the body's kinetic and potential energy to strain energy - via the elongation of elastic elements, mainly tendons - that can be recovered in the propulsive second half of the stance phase (Dickinson et al., 2000; Roberts and Azizi, 2011; Cavagna et al., 1964)
evidence: Supported by citations to Dickinson et al., 2000; Roberts and Azizi, 2011; Cavagna et al., 1964

claim: The elasticity of tendons influences the operating conditions of the muscles, which in turn are associated with their metabolic cost.
source: In addition, the elasticity of tendons influences the operating conditions of the muscles, which in turn are associated with their metabolic cost (Roberts, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Roberts, 2002

claim: For a given muscle force, the metabolic cost depends on the muscle's operating force-length and force-velocity potential.
source: For a given muscle force, the metabolic cost depends on the muscle's operating force-length and force-velocity potential (Bohm et al., 2019; Bohm et al., 2018; Nikolaidou et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bohm et al., 2019; Bohm et al., 2018; Nikolaidou et al., 2017

claim: The force-length-velocity potential determines the number of recruited muscle fibers and thus the active muscle volume.
source: For a given muscle force, the metabolic cost depends on the muscle's operating force-length and force-velocity potential (Bohm et al., 2019; Bohm et al., 2018; Nikolaidou et al., 2017) (fraction of maximum force according to the force-length [Gordon et al., 1966] and force-velocity [Hill, 1938] curves) because it determines the number of recruited muscle fibers and thus the active muscle volume (Roberts, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Roberts, 2002 and references to force-length and force-velocity curves

claim: Quasi isometric contractions close to the optimum of the force-length curve are theoretically most economical for generating a given force.
source: This means that quasi isometric contractions close the optimum of the force-length curve, that is, with a high force-length-velocity potential, are theoretically most economical for generating a given force.
evidence: Based on inference from the relationship between force potential and active muscle volume

claim: The triceps surae muscle group produces muscular work/energy during the stance phase of steady-state running.
source: At the muscle level, it has been shown that the triceps surae muscle group produces muscular work/energy during the stance phase of steady-state running (Lai et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lai et al., 2014

claim: The soleus is the largest muscle in the triceps surae group.
source: The soleus is the largest muscle in this group (Albracht et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Albracht et al., 2008

claim: The soleus does work by active shortening throughout the entire stance phase.
source: The soleus is the largest muscle in this group (Albracht et al., 2008) and does work by active shortening throughout the entire stance phase (Bohm et al., 2019; Bohm et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bohm et al., 2019; Bohm et al., 2021

claim: The vastus lateralis is the largest muscle of the quadriceps femoris muscle group.
source: On the contrary, the vastus lateralis muscle, as the largest muscle of the quadriceps femoris muscle group (Mersmann et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Mersmann et al., 2015

claim: The vastus lateralis muscle operates nearly isometrically despite a lengthening-shortening behavior of the vastus lateralis MTU.
source: On the contrary, the vastus lateralis muscle, as the largest muscle of the quadriceps femoris muscle group (Mersmann et al., 2015), operates nearly isometrically despite a lengthening-shortening behavior of the vastus lateralis MTU (Bohm et al., 2018; Monte et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bohm et al., 2018; Monte et al., 2020

claim: The quadriceps femoris decelerates and supports the body early in stance while the triceps surae accounts for the propulsion later in the stance phase.
source: The quadriceps femoris decelerates and supports the body early in stance while the triceps surae accounts for the propulsion later in the stance phase (Dorn et al., 2012; Santuz et al., 2020; Hamner and Delp, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Dorn et al., 2012; Santuz et al., 2020; Hamner and Delp, 2013

claim: The soleus has shorter fascicles and higher pennation angles compared to vastus lateralis.
source: The soleus and vastus lateralis, as the largest muscles of both muscle groups, show marked differences in their morphological and architectural properties with shorter fascicles and higher pennation angles in the soleus (Bohm et al., 2019; Maganaris et al., 1998) compared to vastus lateralis (Bohm et al., 2018; Marzilger et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bohm et al., 2019; Maganaris et al., 1998; Bohm et al., 2018; Marzilger et al., 2018

claim: A unit of force generated by the vastus lateralis is metabolically more expensive compared to the soleus because of the long fascicles of the vastus lateralis.
source: Because of the long fascicles of the vastus lateralis, a unit of force generated by this muscle is metabolically more expensive (Biewener and Roberts, 2000) compared to the soleus
evidence: Supported by citation to Biewener and Roberts, 2000

claim: The enthalpy efficiency quantifies the fraction of chemical energy from ATP hydrolysis that is converted into mechanical work and depends on the shortening velocity.
source: The enthalpy efficiency (Barclay, 2015) (or mechanical efficiency; Hill, 1939; Hill, 1964) quantifies the fraction of chemical energy from ATP hydrolysis that is converted into mechanical work and depends on the shortening velocity, with a steep increase at low shortening velocities up to a maximum at around 20% of the maximum shortening velocity (Vmax) and a decrease thereafter (Hill, 1939; Barclay et al., 1993; Hill, 1964)
evidence: Supported by citations to Barclay, 2015; Hill, 1939; Hill, 1964; Barclay et al., 1993

claim: The muscle fascicle behavior is strongly influenced by the decoupling of the fascicles from the MTU excursions due to tendon elasticity and fascicle rotation.
source: The muscle fascicle behavior is strongly influenced by the decoupling of the fascicles from the MTU excursions due to tendon elasticity and fascicle rotation (Azizi et al., 2008; Alexander, 1991; Zuurbier and Huijing, 1992; Wakeling et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Azizi et al., 2008; Alexander, 1991; Zuurbier and Huijing, 1992; Wakeling et al., 2011

claim: Proximal muscles like the knee extensors feature less compliant tendons compared to the distal triceps surae muscles.
source: Regarding the vastus lateralis muscle, it was suggested that proximal muscles like the knee extensors feature less compliant tendons compared to the distal triceps surae muscles, thus limiting the decoupling between fascicles and MTU (Farris and Sawicki, 2012; Biewener and Daley, 2007; Biewener, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Farris and Sawicki, 2012; Biewener and Daley, 2007; Biewener, 2016

claim: The experimentally assessed optimal fascicle length for force generation (L0) of the soleus was on average 41.3 ± 5.2 mm.
source: The experimentally assessed optimal fascicle length for force generation (L0) of the soleus was on average 41.3 ± 5.2 mm
evidence: Experimental measurement reported in the Results section

claim: The optimal fascicle length (L0) of the soleus was significantly shorter than L0 of the vastus lateralis with 94.0 ± 11.6 mm.
source: The experimentally assessed optimal fascicle length for force generation (L0) of the soleus was on average 41.3 ± 5.2 mm and significantly shorter than L0 of the vastus lateralis with 94.0 ± 11.6 mm (p<0.001)
evidence: Experimental measurement with statistical comparison reported in the Results section

claim: The forces that corresponded to L0 of soleus and vastus lateralis (Fmax) were 2887 ± 724 N and 4990 ± 914 N respectively.
source: The forces that corresponded to L0 of soleus and vastus lateralis (Fmax) were 2887 ± 724 N and 4990 ± 914 N (p<0.001), respectively
evidence: Experimental measurement reported in the Results section

claim: The assessed Vmax was 279 ± 35 mm/s for the soleus, significantly lower than the Vmax of the vastus lateralis with 1082 ± 133 mm/s.
source: Furthermore, the assessed Vmax was 279 ± 35 mm/s for the soleus, significantly lower than the Vmax of the vastus lateralis with 1082 ± 133 mm/s (p<0.001)
evidence: Experimental measurement with statistical comparison reported in the Results section

claim: The soleus was active throughout the entire stance phase of running while the vastus lateralis was mainly active in the first part of the stance.
source: The EMG comparison showed that the soleus was active throughout the entire stance phase of running while the vastus lateralis was mainly active in the first part of the stance and with an earlier peak of activation (soleus 41 ± 5% of the stance phase, vastus lateralis 35 ± 4% of the stance phase, p<0.001, Figure 1)
evidence: EMG data reported in Results section and shown in Figure 1

claim: The vastus lateralis had an earlier peak of activation compared to the soleus during running.
source: The EMG comparison showed that the soleus was active throughout the entire stance phase of running while the vastus lateralis was mainly active in the first part of the stance and with an earlier peak of activation (soleus 41 ± 5% of the stance phase, vastus lateralis 35 ± 4% of the stance phase, p<0.001, Figure 1)
evidence: EMG data with statistical comparison reported in Results section and shown in Figure 1

claim: The vastus lateralis MTU started to shorten earlier than the soleus MTU during the stance phase.
source: During the stance phase, the MTU of both muscles showed a lengthening-shortening behavior, but the vastus lateralis MTU started to shorten earlier (soleus 59 ± 2% of the stance phase, vastus lateralis 50 ± 2% of the stance phase, p<0.001, Figure 1)
evidence: MTU behavior data with statistical comparison reported in Results section and shown in Figure 1

claim: The soleus and the vastus lateralis fascicle length were clearly decoupled from the MTU length with smaller operating length ranges throughout the whole stance phase.
source: The soleus and the vastus lateralis fascicle length were clearly decoupled from the MTU length with smaller operating length ranges throughout the whole stance phase (Figure 1)
evidence: Fascicle and MTU length data reported in Results section and shown in Figure 1

claim: The soleus fascicles operated at a length close to L0 at touchdown and then shortened continuously until the foot lift-off.
source: The soleus fascicles operated at a length close to L0 at touchdown and then shortened continuously until the foot lift-off (0.994–0.752 L/L0, Figure 1)
evidence: Fascicle length data reported in Results section and shown in Figure 1

claim: The operating length of the vastus lateralis fascicles remained closely above L0 over the entire stance phase.
source: The operating length of the vastus lateralis fascicles remained closely above L0 over the entire stance phase and was on average significantly longer compared to the soleus fascicles (soleus 0.899 ± 0.104 L/L0, vastus lateralis 1.054 ± 0.082 L/L0, p<0.001, Figure 1)
evidence: Fascicle length data with statistical comparison reported in Results section and shown in Figure 1

claim: The stance phase-averaged force-length potential of both muscles was high and not significantly different.
source: The stance phase-averaged force-length potential of both muscles was high and not significantly different (p=0.689, Figure 2)

claim: The average pennation angle of the soleus was significantly greater than that of the vastus lateralis.

claim: The pennation angle of the soleus increased continuously throughout stance, whereas it remained almost unchanged in the vastus lateralis.

evidence: Pennation angle behavior data reported in Results section and shown in Figure 1

claim: The average operating velocity of the soleus fascicles was significantly higher compared to the vastus lateralis.

claim: The vastus lateralis showed an almost isometric contraction throughout stance.

evidence: Fascicle velocity data reported in Results section

claim: The force-velocity potential of the soleus was significantly lower compared to the vastus lateralis during the stance phase.

claim: The overall force-length-velocity potential of the soleus was significantly lower compared to the vastus lateralis during the stance phase.

claim: The soleus had a significantly higher enthalpy efficiency over the stance phase in comparison to the vastus lateralis.

claim: The advantageous operating conditions specific for soleus and vastus lateralis during submaximal running shown for a moderate speed of 2.5 m/s seem to persist at faster running speeds as well.
